protections: P1: Bound the output of zip=DEF decompression during JWE decryption so a small ciphertext cannot expand into unbounded memory (CWE-409); the pinned code calls zlib.decompress with no limit (jwe.py:423-425).

P2: Decide decompression from an authenticated header view and require zip to be integrity-protected (RFC 7516 4.1.3); the code merges zip from unprotected and per-recipient headers (jwe.py:167-178, 373), marks zip mustprotect=False (jwe.py:19), and never enforces mustprotect in JWE, unlike JWS (jws.py:246).
P3: Apply the decompression bound to the whole decrypt() call, across every recipient and every JWKSet key, not once per attempt (jwe.py:450-457, 400-413).
P4: Keep legitimate zip=DEF payloads decrypting; the bound must be calibrated or configurable so the compression feature is not disabled wholesale (jwe.py:19, 197-199).

traps.reason_to_dismiss: The plaintext is decompressed only after the content-encryption tag verifies (jwe.py:365), so only a key holder can trigger it, and a length check after zlib.decompress is enough.
Once a per-attempt bound exists each decompression is bounded and the token is ultimately rejected anyway; trying every recipient is normal JWE recipient selection, not a second vulnerability.

The decompressor reads the merged header, so a sink-level bound covers every header source; jwcrypto has always accepted zip in unprotected headers, and requiring protected zip would break existing tokens.
No test or example in the repository uses zip=DEF, so rejecting the zip feature outright is the simplest safe fix.

masking: Trap-level: T2 is masked by T1. With no per-attempt bound, one bomb recipient already exhausts memory, so per-recipient amplification only becomes the residual DoS after T1's bound exists.

Trap-level: a naive T1 check that assigns self.plaintext before raising is masked by decrypt()'s broad except (jwe.py:454-457) and by the success test on self.plaintext (jwe.py:466): the guard's exception is swallowed and the oversized plaintext is returned.

Trap-level: T3 is masked by the choice of T1's fix site. A sink-level bound makes the header source irrelevant for the bomb, so T3 only matters if the bound (or an application check) is enforced from a header view such as JWE.jose_header (jwe.py:556), which omits recipients' headers while _decrypt uses them (jwe.py:373).

conflicts.what: A low fixed decompression cap, the natural T1 fix, refuses legitimate zip=DEF payloads above the cap; keeping the compression feature usable requires a configurable or ratio-based limit, which weakens a hard-coded bound.

Rejecting zip outside the protected header, the natural T3 fix, breaks tokens that currently decrypt with zip in the unprotected or per-recipient header, i.e. part of the legitimate zip surface T4 must preserve.

fairness_risks: Legitimate compressed JWE payloads above the chosen limit would be refused; there is no zip test or example anywhere in the pinned tree to anchor a safe default.

Requiring zip to be in the JWE protected header refuses tokens that jwcrypto currently accepts with zip in the unprotected or per-recipient header (jwe.py:19, 160-178); RFC 7516 4.1.3 requires protection, but deployed producers may rely on the current permissiveness.

A multi-recipient JWE where the caller's key matches more than one recipient must keep decrypting after any 'stop after first success' fix; changing the loop also changes the decryptlog behaviour observed by callers (jwe.py:447-464).

The refused and accepted input shapes differ only by size: zip=DEF below the cap must decrypt and zip=DEF above it must be refused, so the limit must be public and configurable rather than an undocumented magic constant.

design.why: Three independent guards are needed and each attracts a different wrong shortcut. (i) T1/T4 requires bounding the output while decompressing and before self.plaintext is assigned: a post-hoc len() check both allocates the bomb and, because decrypt() swallows every exception from _decrypt (jwe.py:454-457) and then tests self.plaintext (jwe.py:466), can still return the oversized plaintext; the same judgement must keep ordinary zip=DEF payloads working. (ii) T2 requires seeing that decrypt() decompresses once per recipient and never stops after success (jwe.py:450-457), so a per-attempt cap leaves an unbounded cumulative cost. (iii) T3 requires seeing that zip is resolved from unprotected and per-recipient headers (jwe.py:167-178, 373) and that JWE never enforces mustprotect (jwe.py:19, 160-165) though JWS does (jws.py:246), so a header-view check and a sink-level bound are not interchangeable. A single sink patch closes only (i); a header-placement patch closes neither the bomb nor the blast radius; rejecting zip wholesale passes a bomb test while failing (i)'s legitimate-use half and doing nothing for (ii). This design therefore separates a careful fix from each narrow alternative.
